headline: Bay depression may develop into cyclone Arnab
summary: The Bangladesh Meteorological Department warns of a deep depression that could intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm heading toward India's coast.
details: A deep depression over the Bay of Bengal has intensified and is expected to develop into a cyclone on Monday, according to the Bangladesh Meteorological Department.
If it forms, the system will be named 'Arnab', a name proposed by Bangladesh meaning 'ocean' or 'sea'.
The system is currently centered south of Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Mongla, and Payra ports, with sustained winds of 50km per hour and gusts up to 60km per hour.
The Meteorological Department forecasts that the storm may move north-westwards and eventually cross India's Andhra Pradesh coast as a very severe cyclonic storm by Wednesday.
In response, Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Mongla, and Payra ports have been advised to hoist distant warning Signal No. 1.
All fishing boats and trawlers in the northern Bay of Bengal have been instructed to move closer to the coast and navigate with caution until further notice.
caption:
A deep depression in the Bay of Bengal could soon become Cyclone Arnab.

A deep depression over the Bay of Bengal has intensified and is expected to develop into a cyclone on Monday, according to the Bangladesh Meteorological Department.

If it forms, the system will be named 'Arnab', a name proposed by Bangladesh meaning 'ocean' or 'sea'.

The system is currently centered south of Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Mongla, and Payra ports, with sustained winds of 50km per hour and gusts up to 60km per hour.

The Meteorological Department forecasts that the storm may move north-westwards and eventually cross India's Andhra Pradesh coast as a very severe cyclonic storm by Wednesday.

In response, Chattogram, Cox's Bazar, Mongla, and Payra ports have been advised to hoist distant warning Signal No. 1.

All fishing boats and trawlers in the northern Bay of Bengal have been instructed to move closer to the coast and navigate with caution until further notice.

headline_marked: Nov 1: [[Saint Martin’s Island to reopen to tourists]] with new rules
headline: Nov 1: Saint Martin’s Island to reopen to tourists with new rules
summary: Visitors can travel to the coral island from November 1 to March 15, 2027, but daily visitor limits and environmental fees will be enforced.
details: Tourism restrictions on Saint Martin’s Island, Bangladesh’s only coral island, will be relaxed from November 1 until March 15, 2027.
The decision was made during an inter-ministerial meeting chaired by Environment Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo on October 12.
To protect the island's biodiversity, the average number of tourists visiting the island must not exceed 3,500 people per day.
Every visitor will be required to pay a Tk 100 environmental conservation fee, which will be managed by the Department of Environment.
Tourist vessels will continue to operate from the Nuniyachhara jetty in Cox’s Bazar, but new vessels require prior approval from the environment ministry.
All previously issued directives on environmental conservation remain in force to ensure the protection of the environmentally critical area.
caption:
Planning a trip to the coral island? Saint Martin’s reopens November 1 with a daily cap of 3,500 visitors.

Tourism restrictions on Saint Martin’s Island, Bangladesh’s only coral island, will be relaxed from November 1 until March 15, 2027.

The decision was made during an inter-ministerial meeting chaired by Environment Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo on October 12.

To protect the island's biodiversity, the average number of tourists visiting the island must not exceed 3,500 people per day.

Every visitor will be required to pay a Tk 100 environmental conservation fee, which will be managed by the Department of Environment.

Tourist vessels will continue to operate from the Nuniyachhara jetty in Cox’s Bazar, but new vessels require prior approval from the environment ministry.

All previously issued directives on environmental conservation remain in force to ensure the protection of the environmentally critical area.
